A short clip of independent journalist Whitney Webb is getting attention, and it describes a scenario worth understanding even if you're skeptical. Her argument is that a major cyberattack on banks could be used to move people onto a new kind of digital money.
Below, we cover what she said, what is documented, what the other side says, and why I believe in Bitcoin. One thing up front: in this clip Webb is describing what she thinks is plausible. She is not reporting that an attack is planned, and she doesn't present evidence of one.

What Webb said
Webb is an independent journalist and author who has written about corruption in government and finance. In this clip, she says a bank cyberattack "seems like a very possible scenario" for three reasons:
It would let banks avoid blame. A hack would let banks point to criminals, not their own decisions, if a financial crisis hit.
It could consolidate the banking system. Only the large, "systemically important" banks would survive.
It could move people onto digital money. Banks could say the money in your account was stolen, then offer to replace it with a dollar-backed stablecoin such as USDC, another token, or a central bank digital currency (CBDC), depending on where you live.
Her point about the last scenario is that you would technically choose to accept the new money, but with little real choice. She calls it "coercion to an extreme degree."
She then points to a warning from the Department of Homeland Security about "killware," and to a 2020 simulation by the company Cybereason. The clip ends with the speaker offering a spiritual explanation for why powerful people would do such a thing and saying the answer is Jesus.
What is documented
Killware is a real term. In October 2021, then–DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas told USA Today that "killware," meaning cyberattacks on infrastructure that could kill people, was a growing threat. He pointed to a February 2021 break-in at a water treatment plant in Oldsmar, Florida. Some security experts said at the time that the hype was running ahead of the evidence.
The Cybereason simulation was a training drill. Cybereason is a private security company that has run election-hacking "tabletop" exercises. Reporting describes DHS, Secret Service, FBI and local police officers playing the defenders against Cybereason's staff playing the attackers. We found no reporting confirming that the exercise was built around canceling an election or declaring martial law, so treat that detail as Webb's claim for now.
CBDCs are real, and spreading. A CBDC is digital money issued directly by a central bank. The Atlantic Council tracks them, and it counts well over 130 countries and currency unions exploring one, covering about 98% of global GDP. China's digital yuan is the largest pilot, and the European Central Bank is working toward a digital euro.

The U.S. has banned a Fed CBDC, for now. A January 2025 executive order stopped federal agencies from creating one. The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act then became law on July 11, 2026, without the president's signature. It bars the Federal Reserve from issuing a CBDC, or anything substantially similar, through 2030. Duke University's financial regulation blog notes the ban reaches only a CBDC on a distributed ledger, and it applies only to the Fed.

The ban doesn't cover stablecoins. Private dollar tokens such as USDC are regulated under a separate 2025 law, the GENIUS Act. Webb's scenario names stablecoins as well as CBDCs, and the new law doesn't restrict them.
The other side
Defenders of CBDCs say digital central bank money could make payments cheaper and faster, and that privacy protections can be designed in. Banking regulators also point out that U.S. banks have prepared for exactly this kind of attack. Under an industry standard called Sheltered Harbor, participating banks back up customer account data every night to an encrypted vault that is completely isolated from their own systems, so balances can be restored after a destructive attack. That doesn't prove an attack could never happen. It does mean "your money simply disappears" would be very hard to pull off.
My take (opinion)
I'm a fan of crypto and Bitcoin, and this clip is a good example of why.
Bitcoin runs on a decentralized network that no company or government controls. You can send it straight to another person, anywhere in the world, at any hour, with no bank approving the payment. Standard transfers usually confirm within minutes to about an hour, and the Lightning Network is built for near-instant payments. If you hold your own keys, nobody can freeze your coins or swap them for something else, because no bank record is involved. That is what people mean by "no middleman," and it is why so many believe in it.
It has real limits, though. The price swings a lot. Bitcoin transactions are public on the blockchain, so it is pseudonymous, not private. And if you keep coins on an exchange, you are trusting that exchange. Holding your own keys also means you alone are responsible for protecting them.
Whether or not Webb's scenario ever happens, I think the lesson is simple: don't keep everything inside one system.
